newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Canberra declares "phase two" of economic reforms.
newsitem.headline: Canberra declares "phase two" of economic reforms.

text.p: Australia's conservative government has executed a political backflip in the past week, reinventing itself as an activist administration committed to continuous economic reform.

Prime Minister John Howard first announced big plans to fix the creaking tax system, but later in the week asserted this was merely part of "phase two" of his reform agenda -- a phase that no-one had mentioned since he won the March 1996 election.

Indeed, until last week it seemed that the government, having rushed into a set of reforms in its first year in office, now intended to sit back on its huge majority, waiting inactively for its likely election win in late 1998 or early 1999.

"The government, having strengthened the fundamentals, has now moved to the second phase of its economic strategy," Howard told a business dinner on Friday, drawing together the theme he had been developing all week.

Paradoxically, one new policy to which Howard committed himself was a more interventionist industry policy -- quite at odds with Australia's sporadic, 14-year-old progression towards a market-oriented, small-government economy.
But the prime minister said conventional economic theory justified government intervention.
"My government is prepared to strategically intervene in industry to offset distortions and remove impediments to expansion," he said on Friday.
The Liberal-National administration, which succeeded a 13-year-old Labor government, has slid rapidly in opinion polls this year.
Its lead over Labor is now about five percentage points, compared with the 12 points typical of last year.

It is impossible to be sure why this has happened, but one government insider said on Friday it was probably no coincidence that the administration lost its dominance after it stopped reforming last year and began to look inactive.

A huge attack on Canberra's deficit crowned last year's initiatives, carving 1.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) off the budget and promising a surplus of 0.3 percent of GDP in the fiscal year to June 1999 -- election year.

That budget forecast does not count an expected gush of cash from planned asset sales, particularly the disposal of 33 percent of state telecoms carrier Telstra Corp Ltd, which might raise $10 billion (US$7 billion), about 2 percent of GDP.
Tax reform might be a gamble, however.
Howard himself has previously said that "tax reform" really means a value-added tax -- an intensely controversial policy that was central to the conservatives' 1993 election loss.
The Liberal-Nationals complain that in 1993, Labor ran a scare campaign against their proposal for such a tax, which they called the "goods and services tax" or GST.

Pending a bureaucratic inquiry, Howard will not now commit himself to a GST, but he has made only positive comments about such a policy since he launched the tax initiative on Wednesday. So it seems clear the election will become another referendum on the GST policy.
Labor, whose initial response on Wednesday was ambiguous, is now emphatically opposed to a GST and indeed any tax reform.
Labor treasury spokesman Gareth Evans said on Sunday the government's GST would tax car repairs, child care, hairdressing, movies, football and even funerals.
"Every single one of these things is going to be taxed at 15 to 20 cents in the dollar, depending on the rate that they strike," he said on television.
"We're not in the scare business. We're in the information business. It's just that the information is rather scary."
Critics and business in particular say the current tax system is a mess. Its indirect taxes apply inconsistently to goods, but to services barely at all.
Income tax carries the greatest burden and its top rate near 50 percent applies to incomes just 1.5 times the average wage.
